Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1) succeeds Fable 5 in the same tier at the

feat(gateway): honest readiness probe and a real synthetic check every 30 minutes (#484)

/api/misc/health is the Fly liveness check and has to stay 200 while a
dependency is merely degraded, or Fly restarts a machine that a restart
cannot fix. That is why on 2026-09-02 every rate-limited route answered
500 for two days while health reported 200 "degraded" and nothing noticed.

Add GET /api/misc/ready (and the /misc/ready alias) next to it: one EVAL
through the same @nebutra/cache client the rate limiter uses, one SELECT 1
through the system Prisma client, 503 {ready:false, failing:[...]} when
either is down, 200 {ready:true} otherwise. /health is unchanged and Fly
stays pointed at it. /api/misc is already in the global rate-limit skip
list and outside the /api/v1 metering scope; the skip test now names the
new paths. OpenAPI spec and the web app's generated API types regenerated.

Point the monitors at the honest probe:

- scripts/check-public-urls.mjs gains three request-path targets — the
  readiness probe must be 200 with ready=true, /api/v1/legal/documents must
  be 200 and carry x-ratelimit-limit (the limiter actually ran), and
  /api/system/status must say "redis":"connected" — plus a --critical-only
  flag selecting those and the console.
- public-url-check.yml now has two jobs: `critical` every 30 minutes and
  the `full` daily sweep with aliases at 01:30 UTC, each keyed on
  github.event.schedule with its own concurrency group. Neither installs
  the workspace (the script only needs global fetch). A failed scheduled
  run is the alert channel.
- The public status page (apps/landing status-checks) probes
  NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL/misc/ready instead of /system/status and reads the
  readiness contract: ready=true is operational, a failing database is an
  outage, a failing rate-limit store is degraded. The older status shape
  is still understood.

redis-down=503, db-down=503, both-down, non-1 EVAL, headers, timers);

fix(cursor): stop discarding failed cache moves on account switch (#1258)

`reconcile_cache_files` moves `usage.json` back under the outgoing account
and promotes the incoming account's cache into its place. Both call sites
discarded its error with `let _`, and the function itself aborted on the
first `fs::rename` failure with `?`.

Two things went wrong when a rename failed. The switch was recorded anyway,
so `active_account_id` pointed at an account whose cache was still the other
account's `usage.json`, and the next sync filed one account's usage under
the other. And because `?` returned from the whole function, a failure on
the JSON cache left the legacy CSV cache stranded under the wrong account
without ever being attempted.

Failures are now collected per extension and reported together, so both
caches are always attempted. A failed "move the active cache out of the
way" skips the rest of that extension instead of falling through to the
promotion, which would otherwise overwrite the outgoing account's only copy
with the incoming account's data.

`set_active_account` propagates the error before it mutates anything, so
`run_cursor_switch` no longer prints "Active Cursor account set to ..." for
a switch that did not happen. `upsert_credentials` still saves a freshly
read desktop token — losing that would be a worse outcome — but only points
`active_account_id` at the new account once its cache really is
`usage.json`.

Split out `reconcile_cache_files_in_dir` so the tests can drive a temporary
cache directory, matching the existing `archive_cache_file_in_dir` split,
and switched the internal archive calls to the `_in_dir` variant. Both
resolve to the same directory in production.

Constraint: `sync_cursor_cache` already discards `ensure_credentials_from_local_cursor`, so propagating out of `upsert_credentials` cannot break the sync path
Rejected: Roll the caches back on failure | a partial rollback can fail the same way and would need its own recovery path
Rejected: Keep `let _` and only log | the caller has no way to tell a recorded switch from a stranded one
Confidence: high
Scope-risk: narrow
Directive: The `continue` after the first rename failure is load-bearing — removing it lets the promotion overwrite the outgoing account's cache; `reconcile_cache_files_does_not_promote_over_a_stuck_active_cache` covers exactly that
Not-tested: A rename that fails midway through a real cross-device move; the tests force failure with a non-empty directory at the destination

`VectorStore` is the concrete ChromaDB class; `PgVectorStore` implements the same
method surface and inherits from `object` alone. Both verified by execution:
`PgVectorStore.__mro__` is `[PgVectorStore, object]`, and
`resolve_backend(None, "postgresql+asyncpg://…")` returns `"pgvector"`. So the
assert failed on EVERY production request.

`_rag_artifacts_async` catches Exception, logged at DEBUG, and returned `[]`. So
`pack.rag_chunks` was always empty, `sources.add("rag")` never fired, and answers
were composed with no documentation context at all — with no counter, no event,
no sentence and no trace span saying so. Live since the 2026-08-28 backend flip,
and #263 made `auto` the code default, which extended it to every fresh install
on Postgres.

The assert could not guard what it was pointed at: a NOMINAL isinstance over a
STRUCTURAL contract fails exactly when the contract is honoured by a different
class. The other two call sites pass the same object with no check and work.

Deleting it alone would leave the contract unexpressed — mypy said so, because
the assert had been doing the type narrowing. So the contract is now stated
structurally: `VectorStoreLike`, a Protocol carrying the one method retrieval
consumers call, deliberately NOT `runtime_checkable` — a runtime isinstance over
a structural contract is the defect this exists to prevent. `HybridRetriever` is
typed against it. A Protocol rather than a base class because the two share a
shape and nothing else: `VectorStore.__init__` opens a chromadb client.

Both `except` blocks now log at WARNING. Reaching them means the store RAISED —
an empty result is `chunks = []` and never comes through that branch — so `[]`
still keeps the vision-§7 graceful degradation while the reason stops being
invisible.

Two things the tests caught that I had wrong:

- the DEBUG→WARNING change landed in only one of the two identical handlers, and
  it was the sync leg, not the async one where the bug actually lives;
- the first stub returned no `distance`, and the fused path drops any hit without
  one — `PgVectorStore.query` returns it shaped exactly as ChromaDB does, so the
  test would have passed for the wrong reason.

Evidence: tests/unit/test_catalog_rag_leg_backend_agnostic.py, 4 cases, 2 red
against the old code. Full backend suite 7361 passed, 6 skipped, 1 xfailed. ruff
and mypy (390 files) clean.

fix(lattice): fan out the shard batch read so a wide probe stops timing out (#1920)

* fix(lattice): fan out the shard batch read so a wide probe stops timing out

TraverseForBatchReadAsync awaited one leaf at a time, so a batch read's
latency was the SUM of every bucket's round trip rather than the MAX. A
scattered point-probe over a large tree buckets into many leaves, so the
summed latency walked off the end of the Orleans response deadline and
surfaced as a TimeoutException on ILattice.GetManyAsync.

That is what has been failing the repocontext vector-membership probe:
it batches 256 source-id hashes, which scatter across the membership
tree. It aborted the reconcile's file embedding arm, and it also breaks
list_repos on the live deployment.

The write path (SetManyLocalOnlyAsync) already fans out per leaf with a
documented rationale; only the read path was sequential. This mirrors
that shape exactly - sequential resolve pass (the reference and
leaf-access caches are mutated only there), parallel dispatch,
sequential merge - so it adds no interleaving hazard the write path does
not already carry. A single-bucket shortcut keeps the common case free of
the dispatch array and Task.WhenAll.

Also corrects two comments that are now false: the saga raw-entries path
justified staying sequential by citing this shape, and
MembershipProbeBatchSize claimed a bounded batch 'can never approach the
response deadline', which is exactly what it did.

Test uses an arrival barrier rather than timing, so it cannot flake: all
three leaf reads must be in flight at once, which is only reachable when
every bucket is dispatched before the first await. Verified failed-first
- reverting to sequential reports 'Only 1 of 3 leaf reads were ever in
flight at once'.

* docs: drop a stale issue reference from the probe-size comment

Ten defects from the audit: a crash, a silently wrong log-odds, and eight docs that lie

**`tcren features --metadata` crashed after the whole featurisation pass.** The join's hit rate was
read by indexing the JOINED table with `m.columns[1]`, the metadata's second column by position.
`join_metadata` renames `id` to the join key and prefixes any clashing name with `meta.`, so that
name need not exist -- and a `metadata.tsv` whose header is `epitope, id, iptm` raised
ColumnNotFoundError, before `write_csv`, losing an hour of work. Where the name did survive because
it collided with a FEATURE column, it silently counted the wrong column and reported 2/2 rows
matched when 1 matched. It now counts on a column the join actually added. Driven end to end on
three structures with `id` second: `metadata.tsv: +2 columns, 3/3 rows matched`, exit 0.

**`Joint.log_odds` ignored the column order it documents.** The docstring promises `X` carries the
columns `subset` names "in that order"; `_idx` returns indices in `self.names` order, so the mean
and covariance sub-blocks were permuted against X's columns and the log-odds was silently wrong for
any caller not already in names order. `anomaly_on` honours caller order, so the two disagreed.
Now order-invariant: the same data with subset and columns both reversed returns the same vector,
where before it returned a different one. Shipped scores never moved -- `ScoreModel._subset` always
built in names order -- so this changes no reported number.

**`tcren assess --list-bands` could not be reached.** Its help says "print the frozen band tables,
then exit"; `--features` was required, so it exited 2 on a missing option. `--features` is now
optional with an explicit error when neither is given, and `--list-bands` prints the four tables.

**`tcren recognize -s` wrote a table its own `--features` reader refuses.** No provenance stamp,
unlike `tcren features`, so the guard reported a file written seconds earlier by the same binary as
written by something that does not stamp. Now stamped the same way.

**Six documentation claims a user would act on and get an error or a wrong answer.**
`README.md` opened the first benchmark block with `tcren pipeline --delta`, and there is no
`pipeline` command; `docs/getting-started.rst` offered `P(real)` from `tcren recognize`, removed in
2.26.0; `docs/reliability.rst` printed one transcript that mixes `recognize`'s S line with
`assess`'s ranking and band lines under a single `assess` invocation -- both real outputs were
captured to split it correctly; `docs/performance.rst` timed a "binder P(bind)" stage under a name
2.26.0 deleted; and both `README.md` and `docs/features.rst` said `--all` adds kinetics, where
`FAMILIES` has six and `--all` also adds `potts`, the family that emits `neg_energy`. The `features`
help documented five of the six and is now six.

**`fit-holdout --help` promised a bit-for-bit refit** and named `tcren score` as the command the
frozen model sits behind; it is `tcren assess`, and the bound is a relative 1e-5. Two docstrings in
`score/model.py` cited `tests/unit/test_score_identities.py` at 1e-13; no such file exists and the
assertion is `< 1e-9` in `tests/unit/test_score.py`. That string is published in the API docs.

**Two regression modules read a directory deleted from the repo.** `legacy/data/` is gone and the
oracle CSVs are at `tests/assets/oracle/data/`, so the MHC sweep failed under RUN_BENCHMARK=1 and
eight annotation-parity tests skipped forever on a reason that no longer applied.

**A test named "they are not the same number" passed when they were.** It asserted
`|corrcoef - I|.max() > 0.05`, which is satisfied by CORRELATION -- five identical channels give 1
off-diagonal and pass. It now asserts no two channel vectors are elementwise close.

777 passed, 3 skipped, ruff green. One pre-existing local failure,
`test_pipeline_superimpose_sets_canonical_frame`, is an empty `~/.cache/tcren/data/Canonical2026`
on this machine, not a code defect; it is green on CI.

A repo wired up for a second account on the same forge points at a
~/.ssh/config alias to pick the right key — `git@github-work:org/repo`.
The alias is local to the machine, so a web URL built from it is dead:

    before  https://github-mjolner/MIA-BU-Energy-Utility/melvapro
    after   https://github.com/MIA-BU-Energy-Utility/melvapro

The alias reaches a repo two ways. Written into the remote, or — the case
here — swapped in by a global `url.<alias>.insteadOf` rule, which
`git remote get-url` applies and `git config --get remote.origin.url`
does not. `web_url` reads the config value for that reason and expands
any surviving single-label host through `ssh -G`; a dotted host, which no
alias can be, skips the lookup. `is_https` keeps reading get-url, since
the transport git dials is exactly its question.

The dead host also cost the row its GitHub glyph, `forge_icon` matching on
the hostname — both repos behind the rule get the mark back.

subscriptions.last_commit_message:
Device binding, risk-based step-up, passkeys — and a chart kit to show them with

Three security controls the register listed as absent, built as one vertical
with a Security screen every role can open.

Device binding: a session may be bound to an enrolled device that holds a
secret shown once and stored as a digest. Every request carries a proof bound
to that one token id, in a header the token does not travel in — so a leaked
Authorization header is not enough, and revoking a device refuses every session
on it at the gateway on the next request. What it does not defeat is written
down beside what it does: malware on the enrolled device, and a stolen
database, are both out of scope and say so.

Risk-based step-up: nine signals, each worth points and a sentence a person can
act on. Bands at 35 and 60, set so no single signal can interrupt anybody and
two heavy ones can. An API key is never asked to step up, because it cannot —
an integration that may not do something is told so rather than refused under a
misleading name. Nothing calls a model, a reputation service, or fingerprints a
browser; networks are remembered at /24 or /48, which is a signal rather than a
location history of a named employee.

Passkeys: WebAuthn verified here, with a minimal CBOR decoder and COSE key
parser, ES256 and RS256. Seven checks in order, each a real attack if skipped.
Attestation is deliberately not requested and allowCredentials is always empty,
both stated rather than implied. The tests build real ceremonies — real key
pairs, real CBOR, real signatures — so every refusal is a real attack with one
byte changed.

Driving it over HTTP found three defects the module tests could not:
- a step-up wrote against the User entity, which lives in another project, and
  the ledger correctly refused to move it. STEP_UP_SATISFIED now has its own
  entity.
- the tenancy view was gated on PLATFORM_ADMINISTRATION, which an enterprise
  administrator does not hold, so the one person who should see their company's
  exposure was refused it.
- enrolment did not bind the session it was performed from, so the control
  looked as though it had not worked.

Also a chart kit: fifteen chart types as inline SVG, zero dependencies,
theme-aware, accessible and responsive. It shipped with the exact defect its
own rules forbid — Number(null) is 0, so an unmeasured week was plotted as a
reading of zero — and its tests found it.

40 of 40 mutations caught on the security modules and their wiring, 19 of 19 on
the charts. Full suite 5,136 tests, typecheck clean, console page walk clean.

CI: one build per branch, newest push wins

Two builds were racing for the same `latest` tag. 1.38.0 went into buildx and
sat there for twenty minutes against a two-to-three minute norm for this
repository; 1.39.0 was pushed meanwhile, started, and is on course to finish
first. Whichever finishes LAST writes `latest`, so the slow older build was
about to quietly republish `latest` as 1.38.0 after 1.39.0 had already landed
-- which looks from the outside exactly like the pull being broken again.

A concurrency group with cancel-in-progress makes the newest push cancel the
older one instead. It also stops the plain waste: nobody wants the image for a
commit that is already two commits old.

No version bump: this changes how the image is published, not the game.

Note this cannot rescue the two runs already in flight. They were started from
a workflow file with no concurrency group, so they belong to no group and
nothing will cancel them; 1.38.0's run still needs cancelling by hand if it
has not finished before 1.39.0's.

subscriptions.last_commit_message:
Give each Cursor agent its own model, and check every one of them

Pre-flight moves to Composer 2.5; refining agents and chips stay on Grok 4.6 at
Extra High thinking. The launcher takes a --role and holds the table, so callers
pass no --model at all.

The check had to change with it. It was gated on the model matching one
hard-coded pin, which meant any other model ran with the verification switched
off — asking for composer-2.5 printed the model, exited 0, and never compared it
to anything. So pointing pre-flight at a second model would have quietly removed
the guard that exists to catch a silently dropped effort suffix. The comparison
is now per-role and unconditional, and an override is refused outright unless it
also says what the model should report.

Two things the launcher got wrong on its own: a -fast model was turned away for
missing a --model-shown it would never be allowed to use, rather than for being
fast; and a stream that stops outside the protocol was caught only by its exit
code, when the bare error line at the end of the log is the thing that says so.

Alongside that, three gaps that cost every caller something:

PATH inside an agent is rebuilt from the login profile. Exporting a runtime
ahead of the launcher does not order it — the agent resolves bare `node` to
whatever the profile defaults to, so the runtime was a property of the
operator's dotfiles rather than of the orchestration. --node-bin prepends the
instruction to the prompt, which is the only layer that can carry it. Every
other environment variable propagates untouched; that is written down too, so
nobody plumbs around a problem that does not exist.

cursor-result.sh replaces the parser each caller was writing by hand, and covers
the case those miss: a run killed by the loop detector has no result line at
all, and reporting nothing for it reads as a quiet run rather than a dead one.
--tool-output recovers what the agent's own shell printed.

cursor-chat.sh takes the chat uuid by shape instead of by position, so a banner
on either side cannot become part of an address whose failure only surfaces
later, as --resume opening a new chat.

The gotchas gain the measured envelope: twelve concurrent runs verified clean,
and what the logs actually weigh.

56 checks cover all of it, driven by a stub agent on PATH — no login, no network
and no billed run, so CI holds it. 487 checks, all green.

Make the marker-block generators idempotent on CRLF

Five generators had independently copied the same regex for replacing their
generated block:

    new RegExp(`${OPEN}[\s\S]*?${CLOSE}\n?`)   ...replaced with BLOCK + "\n"

which is not idempotent in this repo, because core.autocrlf=true means the
working tree is CRLF. After the close marker the next byte is \r, so the \n?
matches nothing, the replacement appends its own \n, and the page gains a blank
line. Demonstrated on a scratch copy: the old build-breadcrumbs turns
`CLOSE\r\n` into `CLOSE\n\r\n`, while the fixed one leaves it untouched.

build-pwa and build-theme drifted once per checkout and then stabilised, since
they already guarded on next !== html. build-breadcrumbs, build-privacy-cta and
build-related-games wrote unconditionally, so they drifted on every run --
apps/index.html had accumulated two blank lines. build-breadcrumbs also
rewrote all ~114 indexable pages each run, so a one-page edit arrived as a
hundred-file diff.

Extracts the shared logic to scripts/lib/marker-block.mjs, following the
play-surface.mjs precedent: consume \r?\n after the close marker, emit the
block in the file's own line ending, and escape the markers before
interpolating them into a RegExp. Each caller now writes only when the content
actually changed and reports how many pages were already current.

build-arcade-schema and build-newsletter-cta were already stable and are
unchanged.

Verified: from a clean tree, build-breadcrumbs twice leaves git status empty
and check-site Clean; all five report 0 written on a second pass.

Openotes 2.2.0: the assistant works, and the sandbox is real

The AI assistant shipped broken in 2.0.0 and stayed broken through 2.1.2. It
worked the whole time under `deno task dev`, which is why nobody caught it:
every defect lived in the gap between "all permissions" and the permission
set the packaged binary uses, and nothing ever looked at that gap.

Five defects, each reproduced before it was fixed. A transport error left the
turn hanging forever, because the client overwrote the peer's error handler on
a slot that holds one. The handshake had no deadline, so the common first run
— npx fetching an adapter — looked identical to a hang, with the button
disabled and nothing to cancel. Sign-in was unreachable: the agent list
reported no auth methods and the interface refreshed over the ones the
handshake had just returned, then opened a session anyway and surfaced a raw
JSON-RPC error where a button belonged. The agent could not read a single
note, because the function that registers a note's path had no callers. And
Claude Code was launched under the wrong package's binary, while "installed"
meant "npx exists" — so consent pinned /usr/bin/npx, which can run anything.

Diagnosing that turned up something worse. SECURITY.md described the
subprocess allowlist as an enforced boundary and the code called the manifest
"the real enforcement". Neither was true: the binary was compiled with -A, and
Deno binds a config permission set only when asked with --permission-set. The
allowlist was decorative, and every release could run any program. It is
enforced now, and verified under that set — curl and sh are refused where
before everything was permitted.

The rest, in short. A model picker, built on how each agent actually takes a
model: read out of the packages rather than assumed, which is how it came to
be an environment variable for Claude and a flag for Gemini, and how three
agents ended up with no picker rather than a control that does nothing. The
session modes that were plumbed through four layers with nothing bound to
them. S3 and Box as sync backends, both with real create-if-absent and
compare-and-swap. Koofr, pCloud and Nextcloud through the existing WebDAV
backend rather than as three more API clients.

And two guards, because the pattern behind most of this was a seam that was
written, documented, and never called — `registerAgentNotePath`, the catalog's
`detect`, `ThemeWatcher.refresh`, all dead. A test now asserts the manifest
covers every environment variable read and every program spawned, and a CI
check drives the whole agent path under the shipped permission set instead of
under -A. Both were validated by restoring the original defects and watching
them fail.

Verified at this commit: 304 tests, WebDAV integration 10/10, the ACP check
5/5 in CI under the shipped permission set, the packaged AppImage passing all
six smoke checks, and fmt, lint and check clean.

feat(harnesses): serve Cline, Goose, Aider and Droid, each through the lever its own CLI publishes (#250)

* feat(harnesses): serve Cline, Goose, Aider and Droid, each through the lever its own CLI publishes

The inbound POST /v1/chat/completions that shipped in 6.30.0 unblocked four
coding agents that had no other way to reach this proxy. Three of them use it.
The fourth turned out not to need it, which is the finding of this batch.

Every claim below was read out of an installed copy of the CLI -- Cline 3.0.61,
Goose 1.48.0, Aider 0.86.2, Droid 0.210.0, each installed into a scratch prefix
-- and then confirmed on the wire against a scratch proxy, because the survey
this work came from was wrong about all four in ways that matter.

Cline publishes --config, which moves its whole configuration directory, so MCC
owns ~/.fcc/cline/ and writes one providers.json into it declaring the
openai-compatible provider -- not the openai-native the survey named, which is
OpenAI's own hosted entry, nor openai, which is merely an alias for the one MCC
uses. -P openai-compatible is passed on every launch: with the provider block
written but not selected, Cline fell back to its own hosted account and failed
"Unauthorized". Two further measurements shaped the file. Cline validates
providers.json as a whole and discards it on any surprise -- one unrecognised
root key, or a provider entry missing updatedAt, made it rewrite the settings
as {"provider": ..., "model": "gpt-4o"} and the next run reached
api.openai.com -- so the document is strictly the shape Cline writes for
itself, MCC's own bookkeeping is stripped immediately before the write, and
updatedAt is declared. And its environment fallback for a missing apiKey did
not authenticate a headless run and did not terminate, so the token is literal
in MCC's own 0600 file under ~/.fcc, the Kimi Code precedent. ~/.cline is never
read for a provider or written.

Goose is the one harness in this project with no generated file at all, and
that is a decision. Goose 1.48.0 does have a declared-model mechanism -- a JSON
file under its config directory whose models[] carry context_limit -- but that
directory is Goose's own, holds the user's settings, and Goose publishes no
variable or flag moving the config file alone. So mcc-goose writes nothing
anywhere: OPENAI_HOST plus OPENAI_BASE_PATH=v1/chat/completions compose the
endpoint, GOOSE_PROVIDER and GOOSE_MODEL pick the session, and
GOOSE_CONTEXT_LIMIT carries the ladder's real context window for that model.
Measured with an empty config directory, Goose ran straight through and its own
config.yaml stayed "missing (can create)".

Aider reads two model documents and searches for each in the working directory,
the git root and the home directory, so both flags are passed and MCC owns both
files. The metadata JSON is LiteLLM's model_cost schema -- what the model is;
the settings YAML is a list of ModelSettings records -- what it accepts, which
is what decides whether --reasoning-effort is honoured at all. The second is
constructed with ModelSettings(**entry), so an unknown key raises: the defaulted
record therefore lives only in the first. HarnessCatalogue grew a sidecar for
this, and the sidecar is written as JSON, which yaml.safe_load parses
identically, so there is one atomic writer rather than two encoders.

Droid speaks Anthropic Messages, not Chat Completions. The survey grouped it
with the OpenAI-only CLIs and said to declare generic-chat-completion-api, with
"try anthropic first" as an aside. Trying it settled it: provider "anthropic"
accepts an arbitrary baseUrl, instantiates the bundled @anthropic-ai/sdk
against it and reaches POST <baseUrl>/v1/messages -- this proxy's own native
protocol with no translation in between. --settings is a runtime overlay merged
for that process only, so MCC owns ~/.fcc/droid-settings.json and ~/.factory is
never edited, and the key is Droid's own ${VAR} reference supplied to the child
process. No Factory account is needed for a model MCC routes.

Which URL shape a harness needs is now a registry field rather than a habit.
An Anthropic SDK appends /v1/messages to a root; an OpenAI SDK appends
chat/completions to <root>/v1. HarnessCatalogue.base_url_shape selects between
config/harness_base_url's two resolvers, so getting it wrong fails a test
rather than a launch.

One demonstrated defect is fixed with it, because all four agents expose it.
A request that streamed to completion through /v1/chat/completions or
/v1/responses was logged as "cancelled", while the identical request to
/v1/messages was logged as "success" -- reproducible with plain curl on both
OpenAI surfaces. Both OpenAI adapters return the moment they translate the
terminal event, which closes the capture wrapper while it is suspended on its
last yield, and GeneratorExit was recorded as a cancellation unconditionally.
It now asks whether the stream had already reached its own terminal event: a
reader that stops after the answer finished is not a cancellation, and one that
stops before it still is.

subscriptions.last_commit_message:
refactor(android): ADB gets its tree walk and listing patches from the shared modules instead of its own copies

`cmdr-adb` was written before `cmdr-fs`'s stat-and-listing modules existed, so it carried its own walk and its own listing patcher: ~186 lines re-deriving arithmetic that now has one tested home. `jscpd` named both directly, pairing `volume/scan.rs` against `cmdr_fs::volume::scan_walk` and `volume/mutation.rs` against `cmdr_fs::volume::patching`.

- `volume/scan.rs` is now the `ScanSource` impl and nothing else (159 → 32 lines): one `STAT`, one `LIST`, and the walk, the batch loop, and the conflict matcher come with it.
- `volume/mutation.rs` is the `PatchSource` impl plus three one-line wrappers (110 → 51).

The walk this inherits also fixes a bug the local copy had guarded against by hand and no other backend did: it counts a symlinked directory as one entry rather than walking it. That matters more here than anywhere else, because `/sdcard` is a symlink to `/storage/emulated/0` on every modern Android, so a scan of `/` would otherwise count the same bytes twice.

❌ `MakesDirectories` stays deliberately unimplemented, unlike SFTP and WebDAV. That walk exists for protocols whose create-directory verb makes exactly one level (`MKCOL`), so it spends a request per missing ancestor. The device shell has native `mkdir -p`: `create_directory_all` is one probe plus one verb at any depth, and adopting the shared walk would trade that away. Both `C.md` and `D.md` say so, since the next person to see an unimplemented trait will reasonably assume it was an oversight.

All 65 crate cells pass untouched. `jscpd` drops from five gaining Rust pairs to three; what remains between `volume_impl.rs` files is the `Volume` trait-method signatures every backend repeats, whose one-line bodies now all delegate to the same shared modules.

bd19ab9 (#462) regenerated catalog-summary.json from a CRLF checkout.
Every recorded sha256 was the CRLF hash of its source file, so the
check failed on every LF platform. The four committed values are
exactly sha256(crlf_bytes):

  google-fonts.csv              committed d03194d2…  = CRLF hash
  google-font-licenses.json     committed 7c35e410…  = CRLF hash
  icons.csv                     committed 272ccf0e…  = CRLF hash
  phosphor-icons-upstream.json  committed 81c37fb3…  = CRLF hash

on Windows reproduce the same commit.

- normalize line endings in generate-catalog-summary.py's digest(), so
  the snapshot no longer depends on the checkout
- apply the same normalization in validate_data.py, which independently
  recomputes the hashes and has to agree with the generator
- add .gitattributes pinning src/ui-ux-pro-max/data/*.{csv,json} to LF,
  so a Windows checkout matches the committed bytes in the first place

existing project convention to the two places that were missing it.

digest identically, the committed snapshot must match the normalized
sources, and a simulated CRLF checkout must still produce the recorded
hashes. The third case fails against the pre-fix digest.
